recent_posts.title: Linux on a Mac (but it's 1999)
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on walkthrough of installing LinuxPPC 1999 on an Apple Power Macintosh 9600/300 from 1997. Covers the historical context of PowerPC architecture, the LinuxPPC distro (a Red Hat 5.0 fork), hardware setup using BlueSCSI for SCSI emulation, partition setup with pdisk, the BootX bootloader, and the resulting GNOME 1.0.4 desktop environment. Ends with a reflection on device ownership, computing history, and why exploring vintage Linux still matters today.

recent_posts.title: Three years using GrapheneOS as a daily driver privacy and trade-offs
recent_posts.summary: A personal account of nearly three years using GrapheneOS as a daily driver on Pixel devices, covering why it's a compelling privacy-focused Android alternative. GrapheneOS strips out Google Play Services by default, leaving a minimal 14-app experience that can be selectively expanded. Sandboxed Google Play is available for those who need banking or travel apps, while a fully de-Googled setup is viable for users willing to use alternatives like Signal, F-Droid, and Obtainium. Key trade-offs include no tap-to-pay support, reduced push notification reliability without Google Play, and some GPS app limitations. Standout features include a duress PIN, PIN scrambling, storage scopes, and dramatically improved battery life. The author also candidly criticizes the GrapheneOS team's combative social media behavior while still endorsing the project as the best privacy option on Android.

recent_posts.title: Linux on a Mac (it's not going back)
recent_posts.summary: Asahi Linux enables installing native ARM-based Linux on Apple Silicon Macs through reverse-engineered drivers and a custom installer. The installation process involves partitioning macOS, installing a bootloader, and setting up Fedora Asahi Remix with KDE Plasma. On an M1 MacBook Air, the experience delivers 10-12 hour battery life, solid performance for web development and containers, and basic gaming capability. While some software lacks ARM support and features like Touch ID don't work, the project successfully extends the lifespan of Apple Silicon hardware beyond manufacturer support cycles.

recent_posts.title: Ditching streaming services for physical media and self-hosted solutions
recent_posts.summary: A personal account of abandoning streaming services in favor of physical media (DVDs, Blu-rays, CDs) and paper books. Covers the technical setup for ripping and managing media using tools like MakeMKV, Handbrake, and Jellyfin on Linux, while critiquing algorithmic recommendations and advocating for more deliberate content consumption and ownership.

recent_posts.title: Using rsync for backups, because it's not shiny and new
recent_posts.summary: A practical guide to using rsync for file synchronization and backups between servers. Covers basic syntax (rsync, options, source, destination), essential flags like --dry-run, -av, --delete, and -z for compression. Explains best practices including push vs pull strategies, using dry-run before actual transfers, and handling slow networks with tmux. Notes rsync's ubiquity across Unix-like systems since 1996, its single-threaded limitation, and mentions rclone as a faster alternative for modern use cases.

recent_posts.title: Linux Mom prepping for the LUG like it's 2005
recent_posts.summary: A brief, repetitive post about installing Linux on various devices, referencing Linux User Groups (LUGs) and nostalgic computing culture from the mid-2000s.

recent_posts.title: Tech YouTubers release nerd rock EP about vintage computers and programming
recent_posts.summary: A group of tech YouTubers formed a nerd-rock band called The Stop Bits and released their debut EP 'Return from Interrupt' featuring songs about vintage computers, programming languages like BASIC, the 6502 instruction set, and Linux. The EP was mixed and mastered using a Linux audio toolchain and includes tracks like 'Boot to BASIC,' 'Magic Smoke,' and 'Put Linux On It.' The band will perform at Vintage Computer Festival Midwest.

recent_posts.title: Modding a Commodore 64 for HDMI!
recent_posts.summary: A detailed walkthrough of installing the HD-64 mod kit on a Commodore 64 to add pixel-perfect HDMI output. The mod replaces the RF modulator with an FPGA-based board that intercepts video signals and converts them to digital HDMI with embedded audio. The installation involves desoldering the original RF modulator, installing the VIC-II interleaver, and connecting the HD-64 board. The result is crisp digital video output without lag, making it easier to connect vintage hardware to modern displays while preserving all original functionality.

recent_posts.title: Building a retro website with Eleventy static site generator
recent_posts.summary: A developer shares their experience building a 90s-style website for their band using Eleventy, a modern static site generator. The post contrasts the simplicity of static sites with the complexity of modern dynamic websites, explaining how Eleventy converts Markdown files into HTML while maintaining the nostalgic aesthetic of early web design. The author demonstrates how to set up Eleventy with the base blog starter, customize templates to achieve a retro look, and deploy the site with modern features like RSS feeds and clean URLs.

recent_posts.title: I make all my videos using Linux. Here's how.
recent_posts.summary: Veronica shares her workflow for video production using Linux, detailing her use of Kdenlive for editing, OBS Studio for video capture, and Inkscape for thumbnail creation. She highlights the benefits of open source software and discusses the various hardware and software tools she employs to create high-quality content, emphasizing that Linux is fully capable of media creation tasks.
